claims.claim: Germani argues Martin sticks to the present because it lets him maintain mysteries.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'Now, As We All Know', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: He sticks to the present because it lets him maintain mysteries

claims.claim: Germani observes that facts one would look up in an encyclopedia of Westeros must instead be delivered by the cast, since no such reference exists in the text.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'Now, As We All Know', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: the kind of fact one would look up in the Encyclopedia Westerosica

claims.claim: Germani reproduces Martin's statement that he is a strong believer in telling stories through a limited but very tight third person point of view.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, interview for Adria's News, quoted by Erik Germani, At Sea Journal
claims.quote: telling stories through a limited but very tight third person

claims.claim: Germani finds Martin generally hovering right over his point of view characters' shoulders, then stepping back at odd times.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'The Unseen Plane Crash', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: hovering right over his POV’s shoulders

claims.claim: Germani identifies a passage naming Jaime Lannister in full from Tyrion's viewpoint as the author's voice rather than the character's.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'The Unseen Plane Crash', At Sea Journal
claims.page: essay body, on a breakfast scene

claims.claim: Germani argues Martin keeps readers turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: Martin keeps us turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences

claims.claim: Germani compared authors in his corpus for comparisons of the colour black and found Martin the runaway consumer of the construction.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: Martin was the runaway consumer of the construction

claims.claim: Germani writes that except in cases of emotional shock a reader never has to read a sentence of A Game of Thrones twice.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: you never have to read an AGOT sentence twice

claims.claim: Germani states that the prose constituting the other 60% of the text, beside dialogue, is forgettable.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: the prose that constitutes the other 60% of the text is forgettable

claims.claim: Germani writes that most fantasists settle for a few linguistic relics to give a historical veneer, and names 'must needs', 'soon or late' and 'near as' among Martin's.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'Linguistic Anachronism', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: a few linguistic relics to give a historical veneer

claims.claim: Germani argues that what a fantasy writer needs to build is cultures rather than worlds, and that a culture is before anything else a language and a voice.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'Linguistic Anachronism', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: What we need to do is build cultures, not worlds

claims.claim: Germani argues that it matters what kind of trees a fantasy writer names and what sort of animals.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'Linguistic Anachronism', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: It matters what kind of trees you name, what sort of animals

claims.claim: Germani finds that in A Game of Thrones Martin uses semicolons and colons interchangeably.
claims.quote: Martin uses semicolons and colons interchangeably

claims.claim: Germani reports finding three instances of a semicolon standing where a colon belongs on a single page of his edition of A Game of Thrones.
claims.quote: there are three examples of this on one page
claims.page: essay body, citing p.239 of his edition

claims.claim: Germani likens Martin's paragraphs to Jenga towers from which several sentences can be removed before they wobble.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'Compressible Paragraphs', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: Martin’s paragraphs are like Jenga towers
